Mandate for Leadership, p. 790, trade chapter: "Order the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of Justice to contract with U.S.-owned and U.S.-operated artificial intelligence companies that are capable of detecting, identifying, and disrupting both the domestic groups' and CCP influencers' social media operations and funding streams using public information as a rapidly available offensive measure." The 2023 Mandate mentions artificial intelligence about 16 times and has no AI chapter. (D)
tl.a: Heritage Foundation, Project 2025 (Peter Navarro, "The Case for Fair Trade")

tl.e: DOJ sues to block HPE's $14 billion purchase of Juniper Networks (N.D. Cal. 5:25-cv-00951-PCP). The same day Mike Davis posts on X: "Amen. The Trump 47 Justice Department's Antitrust Division is already off to a strong start. 3 into 2? You must sue." (D, quoted in the states' brief)
tl.a: DOJ Antitrust Division; Hewlett Packard Enterprise; Juniper Networks; Mike Davis

tl.e: Per the court and the states' brief, Davis, Levi, HPE chief legal officer John Schultz and HPE's Gregg Melinson meet DOJ's Omeed Assefi at the Metropolitan Club in Washington to discuss settling the HPE case; HPE's lawyers of record begin talks with Antitrust Division staff only afterward. (D)
tl.a: Mike Davis; William Levi; John Schultz (HPE); Omeed Assefi (DOJ)

tl.e: In his deposition in the HPE Tunney Act case (taken in early 2026), Alford testified that Slater told him Davis said: "If you don't approve this settlement, I will destroy you. I will destroy your job at the DOJ." The account is secondhand (Slater was not deposed); HPE says nothing corroborates it; Davis told the WSJ it was "utter bull." Davis's Sept 2025 texts to Slater, quoted in the states' brief, include "You're a coward. And a clown." (D, as quoted in ECF 487 and ECF 482; R for Davis's denial)
tl.a: Roger Alford; Mike Davis; Gail Slater

tl.e: Gail Slater leaves as head of the Antitrust Division (Politico: stepped down; CNN: fired). Per the states' brief, Davis afterward wrote: "I've done more than anyone here on the big tech antitrust fight. Gail was a disaster. I recommended her hiring. And her firing." (R; D for the quote, Davis Ex. 26)
tl.a: Gail Slater; Mike Davis; DOJ Antitrust Division

tl.e: Per Judge Pitts's order, HPE adviser Arthur Schwartz and John Schultz meet CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis and Under Secretary of Defense Elbridge Colby; Schwartz "later also talked to" CIA Director Ratcliffe; Schultz and CEO Antonio Neri speak with NSA's chief information officer and others at HPE with "individuals connected to the National Security Council." The court: these "undisclosed contacts with national security officials should have been disclosed." (D)
tl.a: Arthur Schwartz; John Schultz (HPE); Antonio Neri (HPE); CIA; DoD; NSA; NSC

tl.e: HPE CEO Antonio Neri gives the RNC $100,000 ($55,700 to its legal proceedings account) while the HPE Tunney Act fight is under way. (D)
tl.a: Antonio Neri (HPE CEO); Republican National Committee

tl.e: DOJ fires Antitrust Division deputies Roger Alford and Bill Rinner for "insubordination" (DOJ via CNN); Alford later testified he was told the firings were "punishment for objecting to the settlement." (R; D for the testimony as quoted in court filings)
tl.a: Roger Alford; Bill Rinner; DOJ Antitrust Division

tl.e: Judge Pitts approves the HPE-Juniper settlement (ECF 482) while finding HPE violated the Tunney Act by not disclosing its contacts with national-security officials and DOJ leadership, and DOJ violated it by not disclosing alternatives it considered; he calls the violations harmless because the intervening states exposed them: "the public would never have known that DOJ leadership overrode the opinions of the Antitrust Division staff." Process complaints go to "independent legal or political action." (D)
tl.a: Judge P. Casey Pitts (N.D. Cal.); Hewlett Packard Enterprise; DOJ

tl.e: L3Harris removes CEO Christopher Kubasik after a board investigation found "conduct inconsistent with" its code of conduct; Sam Mehta becomes CEO. L3Harris runs the FAA's legacy FTI network (contract from 2002, performance to Sept 30, 2032). (R; D for the contract)

Veritas Capital CEO Ramzi Musallam, whose firm owns Peraton (the FAA air traffic control integrator), gives the RNC $442,600 in one day: $132,900 each to its convention, headquarters and legal proceedings accounts, plus $44,300. (D)
tl.a: Ramzi Musallam (Veritas Capital); Peraton; Republican National Committee

tl.e: Checkmate Government Relations registers for HPE on "Issues regarding technology and AI systems." Reuters reports its leader, Ches McDowell, "appears in social media posts hunting with Don Jr. and co-owns a property with him." (D; R for the McDowell tie)
tl.a: Hewlett Packard Enterprise; Checkmate Government Relations; Ches McDowell

tl.e: Trump v. Illinois: Kavanaugh writes officers "must not make interior immigration stops or arrests based on race or ethnicity."
Durbin letter to DHS quotes Kavanaugh concurrence; asks for any "citizen check" guidance.

USPS EO 14399 mail-ballot rule: PI Sept 4; 1st Cir. denied stay Sept 10; second injunction Sept 13; SCOTUS denied stay Sept 14 (26A305), Kavanaugh: applying rule in 2026 "would be arbitrary and capricious."

sb0663: FinCEN finds ~$270M suspicious student-aid activity (~100 SARs since July alert, >20,000 transactions since Feb), referred to law enforcement as "tip-and-lead information"; Education partners with the Task Force; new FAFSA fraud detection tool; release warns fraudsters may use "super intelligence."

Seven federal grand jury subpoenas seeking voter information reach the Nevada Secretary of State's office between Jun 16 and Sept 2, 2026 (three on Sept 1-2); DOJ declined comment; Secretary Aguilar: "If they can take me out in '26, they have control in '28."

D. Mass. denies the government's motion to transfer California v. Trump to D.D.C. (Apr 28, 2026; 2026 WL 1161857): defendants had not shown the first-to-file rule applied or that transfer served the interest of justice.

D. Mass. grants the states summary judgment (Jun 25, 2026; challenged sections of EO 14399 violate separation of powers); the injunction quoted in HSI's Jul 6, 2026 report bars defendants from implementing Sections 2, 3 and 5 as to the plaintiff states (AZ, CA, CO, CT, DE, DC, IL, PA, ME, MD, MA, MI, MN, NV, NJ, NM, NY, NC, OR, RI, VT, VA, WA, WI) for the Nov 3, 2026 election, including any attempt to "create a new federal program to superintend and control Plaintiff States' maintenance of their voter rolls" or to investigate state officials, and requires defendants to "cease and reverse any implementation"; it does not bar citizenship-verification help "at the request of any State and within the framework provided by Congress." Enjoined Sec. 2 is "Establishment and Transmission of State Citizenship Lists and Prioritization of Investigations and Prosecutions Related to Election Fraud." Claims about elections after Nov 3, 2026 were dismissed Jun 18.
tl.a: D. Mass. (Judge Talwani), California v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-11581

tl.e: USPS publishes its EO 14399 ballot-mail final rule (FR 2026-17238; effective date listed Aug 21): states are to give USPS a list of mail voters through a Federal Ballot Mail Portal "to the extent practicable" at least 30 days before the election (the EO said 60), and ballot mailings to people not on the list "will not be accepted." A D. Mass. 14-day TRO blocks most sections Aug 27; Judge Talwani's preliminary injunction follows Sept 4, and it stays blocked through Sept 17. The TRO bars USPS from implementing most of the rule, including its design standards and the refusal of noncompliant outbound ballots (CRS). The Supreme Court denies a stay Sept 14 (R); mismatched mailings would be "kicked back to the county" (NACo).

Boasberg partially grants discovery in the Democrats' VRA suit and orders DOJ to identify, by noon Oct 30, every state it has sent demands since Jul 1 to remove specific voters, set aside ballots or refuse to issue ballots; plaintiffs may update standing Oct 31; ruling on a TRO barring more letters promised by Nov 2 unless DOJ moots it by saying it will send no more before the election.

Opinion denying the DSCC TRO for lack of standing records that "on October 31, discovery in this case revealed that the federal government has sent formal demand letters only to Washington and California" (citing ECF 29-31). "Even extraordinary merits questions cannot justify the extraordinary relief of a preliminary injunction ... if those seeking it lack standing"; the government sent letters "attempting to browbeat" states.
tl.a: Chief Judge Boasberg (DSCC v. Trump, D.D.C. 1:26-cv-03674, ECF 33-34)

tl.e: DOJ's late-Sunday filing before Judge Boasberg argues the Democrats lack standing because the administration's efforts have failed: its letters have no force on their own, "absent the intervention of a federal court, nothing will change with regard to any election procedures"; "State governments have refused to comply with the DOJ's letters" (more than 30 states refused voter data); "Expedited discovery has now come and gone" (R).

DOJ asks Boasberg to consider contempt against CHIRLA and its lawyers over the UCLA analysis of the 20,000-name DHS list, and suggests he refer the matter to DOJ for a possible criminal contempt investigation; calls the analysis "political grandstanding" with "no relevance" to standing. UCLA: counsel and experts "fully complied with the Court's orders." No ruling (R).
tl.a: DOJ (CHIRLA v. DHS, D.D.C., Chief Judge Boasberg)

tl.e: In CHIRLA v. DHS (D.D.C. 1:26-cv-03072-JEB, ECF 48), Chief Judge Boasberg grants in part a TRO/preliminary injunction: Defendants may not "issue demands to California election officials seeking to compel the segregation of ballots, or other deviations from existing state elections procedures, based on voters' inclusion on the lists of suspected non-citizens." The Executive Branch "has likely violated the Constitution's Elections Clause"; 18 U.S.C. 611(a) "does not regulate the time, place, or manner of elections"; DOJ's aiding-and-abetting theory is "a red herring," and its role under 611(a) "is limited to prosecuting non-citizens who 'knowingly' cast ballots." The court finds CHIRLA's expert "well qualified and credible": at least 22 citizen members are certain matches to the DOJ list, 66 near-certain, and 6,140 CHIRLA citizen entries are "at risk" under probabilistic criteria. DOJ had sent demands and lists to all 58 counties; some counties are reviewing the lists. DOJ told the court its letters are "not self-executing" but recipients ignore them "at their own legal peril." DOJ's motion to strike and for sanctions (ECF 45) is left pending. $1 bond.

Boasberg dismisses or denies relief in DSCC v. Trump for lack of standing: "Even extraordinary merits questions cannot justify the extraordinary relief" sought; notes the "modest relief" granted the same day in CHIRLA v. DHS.

Late Nov 2 a 2-1 Ninth Circuit panel (Bea, Callahan) stays Thompson's TRO in SEIU v. DOJ, calling DOJ's letters and warnings "core Executive functions"; Chief Judge Murguia dissents. Hours later a majority of active judges votes to rehear en banc, vacating the panel order; the en banc court will decide DOJ's stay request. The TRO remains in place.
tl.a: Ninth Circuit (Bea, Callahan; Murguia dissenting; en banc court)

tl.e: Around noon PT on Election Day, the en banc Ninth Circuit voted 6-5 to reinstate the Nov 2 panel order staying Judge Thompson's TRO "pending further order of the court": "A majority of the en banc court has voted to reinstate the three-judge panel's order filed on November 2, 2026." DOJ may again ask officials to set aside ballots of listed voters while citizenship is checked, and warn that tabulating them could bring prosecution, including aiding-and-abetting liability (states need not comply). The stay also lifts the TRO's requirement that DOJ disclose pending search-warrant applications and grand-jury subpoenas. Dissents: Chief Judge Murguia, Judge Desai. Essayli: "The rule of law prevails. Separation of powers does not allow judges to take control of core executive branch powers"; DOJ "will conduct our criminal investigations without fear or favor."
tl.a: Ninth Circuit (en banc), SEIU v. DOJ, No. 26-7303

tl.e: Text of the en banc order now read (upgrades to D): "A majority of the en banc court has voted to reinstate the three-judge panel's order filed on November 2, 2026. Pending further order of the court, the three-judge panel order ... is reinstated." Concurrence (Miller, joined by Bennett): a district court "does not generally have the authority to enter an injunction prohibiting the Department of Justice from expressing its views about criminal statutes." Dissent (Chief Judge Murguia, joined by Gould, Owens, H.A. Thomas, Desai): "The majority permits Defendants to preempt state election procedures by threat of prosecution"; records that letters were delivered "using uniformed DHS officers" and "Federal marshals reportedly served at least one county employee at home." Desai: the stay came "just after the polls open on Election Day." The reinstated panel order stays the TRO term requiring DOJ to disclose pending search-warrant applications and grand-jury subpoenas.
tl.a: Ninth Circuit (en banc), SEIU v. DOJ, No. 26-7303 (DktEntry 32.1)
